column2: Though memories of Napoleon's campaign in Egypt and the Levant thirty years ago are fading, one vestige remains: the Jewish concession in Acre Sanjak, established after Napoleon's failed attempt to gain Jewish support by promising autonomy throughout Palestine. Thanks to the intervention of Galilean Jewish bureaucrat Haim Farhi, the Sultan granted Jews the right to immigrate to Acre and set up autonomous institutions. Today, the Acre Sanjak welcomes Jewish settlers willing to invest and risk the journey--an act known as aliyah, meaning "ascension" to the Land of Israel--with some aspiring to fulfill messianic prophecy by restoring Jewish sovereignty after 2,000 years. Could this ambitious dream become reality?

Israel normally spawns as a mid- to late-game tag as a result of a great power releasing it either in Palestine or another location in the by the 1890s and as late as the 1920s. This option enables you to play as Israel at the game's start. You can choose to start under either a semi-realistic alternate history scenario as an Ottoman or Egyptian vassal able to become independent eventually, or as a immediately independent Israel in Palestine.

The Galilee's abundant fertile grassland and freshwater is critical for our country's agriculture. Within the northernmost portion of the Galilee, though, lies Lake Hula--which, despite its obvious potential as a water source, is a breeding ground for malaria along with its surrounding marshland where mosquitoes breed in abundance. We must drain Lake Hula and further expand our land cultivation in the North--it's an obvious and highly profitable investment.
Choose a Starting Scenario for Early Israel

\n\nThere are two available starting scenarios for early Israel: one as an Ottoman or Egyptian vassal in the Acre Sanjak and the other as a fully independent Jewish state in all of Palestine. The former has more flavor, adapted to the timeline as would be fitting, while the latter offers the player more free reign to expand without scripted civil wars and defensive wars with their neighbors.
Draining the malaria-infested Lake Hula, converting it into an arable valley, has allowed us to greatly expand agriculture operations in the Upper Galilee.

As Jewish immigration to the Palestine Vilayet accelerates, land purchases from absentee landlords have enabled new settlements to take root--but at a notable humanitarian cost. Long-established Arab tenant farmers, known as fellahin, are being evicted to make way for Jewish arrivals, provoking growing resentment among them and their urban Arab brethren. Their displacement has stirred unrest that could pose serious challenges to stability as Jewish rural settlement expands. In light of this, we have a three-way choice. We may press forward with land acquisitions regardless of the fallout, limit the number of fellahin evicted at a time to ease tensions, or pivot toward urban settlement to minimize rural displacement altogether.

We are prioritizing settling as many Jews as possible in the Palestinian countryside, with no limit to how many fellahin will be evicted from farms purchased from absentee landlords. This will cause significant unrest among the fellahin and their Arab brethren, but it's a small price to pay for hastening the exiles' return to Eretz Yisrael.

We have set a reasonable limit on how many fellahin may be evicted at once whenever Jewish patrons purchase farmland from absentee landlords, even though these purchase indeed continue. This allows us to strike a balance between our goal of settling as many Jews as possible in the Palestinian countryside and our need to maintain the peace. Arab agitation, however, persists.

In a bold initiative, the German American Jewish organization B’nai Brith has announced its launching of a resettlement scheme for German Jews within the Palestine Vilayet. This effort marks a huge divergence from the organization’s original purpose as a means of helping German Jewish immigrants adjust to life in America, as well as advocating for their dignity in their adopted home. Now that the return to Zion is being realized at an unprecedented level, the organization will seek its own contribution to it. They will purchase arable land in Palestine and organize group emigrations, both from Germany and the United States. It remains to be seen how many Jews will emigrate on B’nai Brith’s dime, but we have every right to be optimistic that many will answer the call.

The Jewish community in Palestine will not survive if it does not have a centralized, well-armed defense force. While incoming Jewish settler communities so far have formed their own loosely organized group of armed watches, known collectively as HaShomer, their men do not answer to a central command and are by no means armed enough for potential war with the Arabs or external threats. It is time for the Jewish people to have their own army again--as ferocious as the Maccabees, as adept in battle as King Solomon's sixty warriors!
